title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
NoteReproducibility



Every figure in this paper is produced by one of two executed notebooks: missing_data_analysis.ipynb (Part I) and rural_severity_model.ipynb (Part II). The script project-site/scripts/export_assets.py copies their figures into project-site/assets/. Key numbers quoted in the text are kept in _variables.yml.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
2.1 Data-quality findings

Inconsistent names. The MAR file calls the hour column HOUR (MNAR: HOUR_OF_DAY), and the MNAR file’s worksheet is named MCAR_ex1. Both are harmonized on load.
Spreadsheet debris. Rows 1000–1029 of features.xls have no outcome and at most two filled cells. They are removed.
Duplicated crashes. LANE_COUNT and SPEED_LIMIT come from PennDOT’s ROADWAY table, which holds one row per road involved. When it is joined to the crash data, a crash on several roads appears several times. The 1,000 rows are only 679 distinct crashes (224 crashes appear 2–5 times; Section 4.1). This matters for any model evaluated by cross-validation.
Undocumented codes. URBAN_RURAL = 4 (421 crashes) is not defined in the dictionary (only 1–3 are), and URBAN_AREA is not documented at all. The RURAL flag, which equals URBAN_RURAL = 1 exactly, is used instead.
Outliers. PERSON_COUNT = 48 is a genuine school-bus crash and is kept. PERSON_COUNT = 0 is implausible for a reportable crash and is flagged. HOUR_OF_DAY and SPEED_LIMIT contain no out-of-range values.







Figure 1: PERSON_COUNT outliers. The 48-person value is a real school-bus crash; values of 0 are implausible.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
3.1 Missingness mechanisms
Let \(R\) indicate which values are observed, and split the data into observed and missing parts, \(Y = (Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}})\). Following Rubin (1976) and Little and Rubin (2019):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{MCAR:}\quad & P(R \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}) = P(R) \\
\text{MAR:}\quad  & P(R \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}) = P(R \mid Y_{\text{obs}}) \\
\text{MNAR:}\quad & P(R \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}) \text{ depends on } Y_{\text{mis}}
\end{aligned}
\]
Under MAR, missingness may depend on variables we can see (including the outcome) but not on the hidden value itself. MNAR cannot be detected from observed data alone, because the evidence is exactly what is missing. We can test it here only because the hidden values can be recovered (Section 3.2).
Table 2 summarizes the gaps. Only WET_ROAD, YOUNG_DRIVER and PERSON_COUNT are affected, and PERSON_COUNT is missing in the same 69 rows in both files. The two files differ in the shape of missingness. In MAR the gaps are scattered, so 38.5% of rows have at least one. In MNAR, WET_ROAD and YOUNG_DRIVER are always missing together (224 rows with both, 10 with all three), so more cells are missing (537 vs. 453) but fewer rows are affected (29.3%).

Because each hides different cells, combining them recovers the true value of most gaps. The remaining 44 WET_ROAD and 49 YOUNG_DRIVER cells are missing in all three files. title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
section: 3.3 Treatments and their effect on the data
text:
3.3 Treatments and their effect on the data
Each file is treated three ways:

mean imputation: replace each gap with the column mean;
median imputation: replace each gap with the column median;
complete-case (CC) removal: drop every row with any gap.

Figure 3 and Figure 4 compare the original and treated distributions side by side, with the reference marked by black diamonds. Two artifacts are immediately visible. Mean imputation creates values that cannot occur (e.g. WET_ROAD = 0.13). Median imputation sets every missing yes/no value to “no”, because the median of a rare flag is 0.






Figure 3: MAR: distribution of every variable, original vs. each treatment. ◆ = reference; hatched bars = imputed values; gray = missing.









Figure 4: MNAR: the same comparison.



Figure 5 summarizes the distortion of each variable’s mean.

Mean imputation reproduces the observed mean exactly. Under MAR that is nearly unbiased. Under MNAR it inherits the observed-data bias (wet roads −8%, young drivers +6%).
Median imputation understates wet roads by 19% (MAR) and 30% (MNAR), and young drivers by 18–19%.
Complete-case removal keeps 615 (MAR) or 707 (MNAR) rows. It lowers the fatal/serious rate from 5.1% to 4.6% (MAR) and 4.4% (MNAR) because the removed rows were disproportionately severe. Under MAR it discards 23 of the 51 severe crashes.







Figure 5: Percent difference of each variable’s mean from the reference, by treatment.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
3.4 Logistic regression on every dataset
We fit \[
\operatorname{logit} P(\text{severe}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{SPEEDING} + \beta_2\,\text{WET\_ROAD}
+ \beta_3\,\text{YOUNG\_DRIVER} + \beta_4\,\text{HOUR\_OF\_DAY} + \beta_5\,\text{PERSON\_COUNT}
\] on each treated dataset and on the reference (Hosmer, Lemeshow, and Sturdivant 2013). Because only 5.1% of crashes are severe, an unweighted model predicts “not severe” for everyone: 94.9% accuracy and F1 = 0. We therefore use balanced class weights, which trade accuracy for the ability to find severe crashes. Performance is estimated with stratified 5-fold cross-validation repeated 20 times. The original (untreated) files cannot be fitted directly; standard software silently drops incomplete rows, which is complete-case analysis.
We run two evaluations. In the first, each model is scored on its own treated data. In the second, a fair head-to-head, each model is trained on treated training rows (imputation statistics from those rows only) and scored on the true reference values of the same held-out rows (Table 5).

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
3.5 Part I findings

Complete-case removal is the most biased treatment under both mechanisms, and markedly so under MNAR. The removed rows are systematically different (wetter roads, more severe crashes), so deleting them shifts the outcome rate, distorts coefficients and widens every interval.
Mean imputation is the least biased simple method overall. It preserves variable means (exactly, under MAR) and keeps coefficients close to the reference. It does create impossible fractional flag values and shrinks variance.
Median imputation should not be used for binary predictors. It silently recodes every gap as “no”, the largest distortion of the predictor distributions. Its coefficient error is similar to mean imputation.
Under MNAR, every simple treatment stays biased. A method that uses only observed values cannot know that the hidden roads were wetter.
Better than any imputation: recover the values from source fields (Table 3), or use multiple imputation with auxiliary variables and missingness indicators (Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn 2011), plus a sensitivity analysis for MNAR.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
4.1 Cleaning and the rural lens
Part II uses all 80 columns of features.xls. Three cleaning steps matter:

Collapse duplicated crashes. Consecutive rows that agree on every non-roadway column (at least 60 columns compared) are one crash. None of the merged crashes has a conflicting time of day, and 161 of them differ in SPEED_LIMIT/LANE_COUNT, as expected for multiple roads. Crash fields take the first non-missing value, and roadway fields take the maximum (the fastest road involved). This leaves 679 crashes, of which 36 are severe (5.3%). Without this step, copies of one crash would land in both training and test folds.
Rebuild calculated flags. WET_ROAD, YOUNG_DRIVER, DRIVER_20YR, DRIVER_50_64YR and MULTIPLE_VEHICLE are rebuilt from complete source fields (99.6–100% agreement with known values).
Drop duplicate and undocumented columns (TIME_OF_DAY, ILLUMINATION, URBAN_RURAL, URBAN_AREA). Remaining gaps are mean-imputed inside each training fold.







Figure 7: Rows per crash before deduplication.



Rural lens. Only 11 of 177 rural crashes were severe. A common guideline asks for about ten outcome events per predictor (Peduzzi et al. 1996), so ten features on rural crashes alone would be unstable. We therefore train on all crashes and apply the rural lens at every step: the filter is run on rural crashes separately, rural evidence enters the final selection, the model is evaluated on rural crashes alone, and conclusions are drawn for rural roads.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
4.2 Feature selection
Step 1: first principles. Crash severity is the energy that reaches a human body, relative to what that body can tolerate. Each column is assigned to a mechanism, or rejected:

Rejected columns: administrative and calendar fields (county, month, day of week), undocumented or duplicate codes, and AUTOMOBILE_COUNT (a proxy for vehicle mix with no mechanism of its own). RURAL is the analysis lens, not a predictor, because it is constant on rural roads. No remaining column records the outcome, so there is no leakage.
Step 2: a simple filter. Each candidate is tested on its own, on all crashes and on rural crashes. For flags we report the risk ratio \[
\text{RR} = \frac{P(\text{severe} \mid \text{flag} = 1)}{P(\text{severe} \mid \text{flag} = 0)}
\] with Fisher’s exact test (Fisher 1922); numeric features use the Mann–Whitney test (Mann and Whitney 1947). A feature passes if it is exposed in at least 15 crashes and has p < 0.20 in either group. The threshold is loose because this is screening, and with 36 events a strict cut-off would discard real effects.






Figure 8: Risk ratios of the flags that pass the filter, all crashes (●) vs. rural crashes (■). Faded = p ≥ 0.20 in that group.



Step 3: redundancy and the final pick. Several passing flags carry the same information. ALCOHOL_RELATED is identical to DRINKING_DRIVER, and both sit inside IMPAIRED_DRIVER. RUNNING_STOP_SIGN and RUNNING_RED_LT are entirely contained in AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING. SUDDEN_DEER ≈ DEER_RELATED. We keep the umbrella flag in each case. SPEEDING is also contained in AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING, but it is kept for its distinct energy mechanism and its strong signal. Combining filter rank, first-principles strength and rural evidence gives the final ten (Table 8). ILLUMINATION_DARK was chosen over LEFT_TURN, the next by overall p-value, because of its stronger rural signal and its core mechanism.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
4.3 Multicollinearity
The largest pairwise correlation among the ten features is 0.29 (ILLUMINATION_DARK with IMPAIRED_DRIVER; impaired driving is mostly at night). Every variance inflation factor, \(\text{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2)\), is below 1.25, far from the usual warning levels of 5 and 10. By contrast, the top ten by p-value alone, without the redundancy step, contains identical columns with infinite VIF (Figure 10).









Figure 9: Correlations among the selected features.











Figure 10: VIF: selected ten (left) vs. top ten by p-value without redundancy removal (right).







4.3.1 Pairwise association tests
As a pair-by-pair check, we also apply the two standard association tests. Pearson’s \(r\) is used for pairs of continuous or count variables. For pairs of categorical (yes/no) variables, we run a chi-square test on their contingency table and measure strength with Cramér’s V, \[
V = \sqrt{ rac{\chi^2}{n\,(\min(r, c) - 1)}},
\] which for two yes/no variables equals \(|\phi|\). The two numbers answer different questions. The p-value tests the null hypothesis that the variables are independent: a small p-value means they are associated, and with hundreds of crashes even a weak link is significant. The strength (\(|r|\) or V) decides redundancy: above 0.8, drop one of the pair; 0.7–0.8 is marginal; below 0.7, keep both.
Worked example. For AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING × ALCOHOL_RELATED, alcohol crashes are less often aggressive than independence would predict: 14 observed vs. 22.1 expected. \(\chi^2 = 6.65\), df = 1, p = 0.010, so the two are associated. But V = 0.10, a weak association, so both are kept.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
4.4 Feature analysis
Figure 13 shows the severe-crash rate with and without each factor, for all crashes and for rural crashes. On rural roads, half of motorcycle crashes and 40% of speeding crashes were severe.






Figure 13: Severe-crash rate when each factor is present (colored) vs. absent (gray), all crashes and rural crashes.



How rural crashes differ. Deer strikes are four times as common in rural crashes (16% vs. 4%), and none of the 49 was severe. Non-collision events are 2.8× as common. Rear-end and distraction crashes are about half as common, which helps explain the higher rural severe rate (6.2% vs. 5.0%). The main risk factors (aggressive driving, impairment, speeding, drivers aged 75+) occur about as often on rural roads as elsewhere.
Why darkness looks protective. First principles say darkness should raise severity, yet dark crashes were severe less often (3.1% vs. 6.0%). The crash mix explains it: motorcycle crashes happen almost entirely in daylight (4.5% of daylight crashes vs. 0.7% of dark ones), and dark crashes are twice as often deer strikes. Darkness is a useful predictor here, but the association is not causal.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
4.5 The final model
Model. Logistic regression on the ten features, with mean imputation and standardization learned inside each training fold, balanced class weights and a mild L2 penalty. The penalty is needed because three features have zero severe crashes, which would push unpenalized coefficients to −∞ (complete separation; Firth (1993) discusses penalized alternatives).
Threshold. The probability cut-off is tuned to maximize F1, where \(F_1 = 2\,\text{precision}\cdot\text{recall}/(\text{precision}+\text{recall})\). It is chosen by an inner cross-validation within each training fold, so the test fold never influences it (median threshold 0.75).
Evaluation. Stratified 5-fold cross-validation repeated 20 times (100 test folds), reported for all crashes and for rural crashes alone.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
section: 4.6 Which factors matter most on rural roads?
text:
4.6 Which factors matter most on rural roads?
For interpretation, the ten-feature model is refitted on all crashes without class weights, keeping the mild penalty. 95% intervals come from 1,000 bootstrap resamples (Figure 16). For the three zero-severe flags, the direction is certain (no resample puts them above 1), but their size is set mostly by the penalty.






Figure 16: Odds ratios with 95% bootstrap intervals.



How much a factor contributes to rural severe crashes depends on its odds ratio and on how often it occurs. The population attributable fraction (Miettinen 1974) among the severe rural cases is \[
\text{PAF} = p_c \,\frac{\text{OR} - 1}{\text{OR}},
\] where \(p_c\) is the share of severe rural crashes with the factor.






Figure 17: Estimated share of severe rural crashes attributable to each risk factor.




Aggressive driving contributes the most. It appears in about half of rural crashes and in 9 of the 11 severe ones, accounting for roughly a third of them (PAF ≈ 36%), despite a moderate odds ratio of 1.8.
Motorcycles are the most dangerous single factor (OR ≈ 4.6, 95% CI 1.6–10.6), the only factor whose interval clearly excludes no effect.
Impairment and speeding each raise the odds about 2.4× and account for about 10% of severe rural crashes each.
Drivers aged 75+ and non-collision events each raise the odds about 1.8×. Non-collision events are 2.8× more common on rural roads.
Low-risk rural crashes are deer strikes (common, never severe), and rear-end and distraction crashes (mostly non-rural).

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
Two questions

Crash databases are incomplete and messy. How we handle that changes the answer to “what makes a crash deadly?”
Part I: missing data. On the same 1,000 crashes, missing at random (MAR) vs. not at random (MNAR): how do mean, median and complete-case treatments bias a logistic regression?
Part II: rural severity. With first principles + a simple filter, which ten factors best predict fatal / serious-injury crashes, and which matter most on rural roads?
Outcome: FATAL_OR_SUSP_SERIOUS_INJ, rare (≈ 5% of crashes).

Data: PennDOT crash records and data dictionary.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
Data and data quality



MAR_ex1.xls, MNAR_ex1.xls: the same 1,000 crashes, 6 columns, different gaps.
features.xls: 80 columns of crash, flag and roadway fields.
The 1,000 rows are only 679 crashes. The ROADWAY join repeats a crash once per road.
URBAN_RURAL = 4 is undefined. PERSON_COUNT = 48 is a real school-bus crash; = 0 is implausible.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
Two kinds of missingness



MAR: gaps depend only on what we can see. MNAR: gaps depend on the hidden value itself.
MAR: scattered gaps → 38.5% of rows incomplete.
MNAR: WET_ROAD and YOUNG_DRIVER vanish together → 29.3% of rows incomplete.
Rows missing WET_ROAD are more often severe (≈ 7.5% vs. 4.5%).

text:
Which treatments distort the data?


Median turns every missing yes/no into “no”: wet roads −19% (MAR), −30% (MNAR).

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
Accuracy and F1 barely differ

No weighting: 94.9% accuracy, F1 = 0 (the model predicts “not severe” for everyone). We use balanced class weights.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
Part I take-aways

Complete case = most biased, especially under MNAR (drops severe crashes; ~2× coefficient error).
Mean imputation = least biased simple method (exact means under MAR).
Median imputation distorts yes/no variables (every gap becomes “no”).
Under MNAR, no simple method is unbiased.
Best fix: recover values from source fields (ROAD_CONDITION, driver-age counts), or use multiple imputation.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
Cleaning and the rural lens

Deduplicate: 1,000 rows → 679 crashes (36 severe, 5.3%). This prevents copies of one crash from appearing in both training and test folds.
Rebuild flags from complete source fields (99.6–100% agreement).
Rural lens: only 11 of 177 rural crashes were severe, too few for a 10-feature rural-only model (≈ 10 events per feature needed). So we train on all crashes, then filter, evaluate and interpret for rural roads.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
section: Feature selection: first principles + a simple filter
text:
Feature selection: first principles + a simple filter



First principles: keep columns with an injury mechanism (energy, unprotected user, crash geometry, impairment, frailty, environment). 73 candidates.
Filter: Fisher’s exact test and risk ratio per flag, on all and rural crashes; pass if p < 0.20 and ≥ 15 exposed.
Redundancy: keep the umbrella flag (IMPAIRED_DRIVER ⊃ drinking/alcohol; AGGRESSIVE_DRIVING ⊃ stop-sign/red-light).

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
Association tests: Pearson and chi-square





p-value = is there any association? (small p → associated). Strength (\(|r|\) or Cramér’s V) = is one redundant? > 0.8 drop one, 0.7–0.8 marginal.
Aggressive driving × alcohol: p = 0.010 (associated) but V = 0.10 → keep both.
Final ten: 19 of 45 pairs significant, max V = 0.29 → keep all.
Pearson: only vehicle count × total units r = 0.97 (neither selected).
Redundant flags removed in selection: V = 0.88–1.00.

section: Where the model succeeds and misses
text: Where the model succeeds and misses

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
What drives severe rural crashes







Aggressive driving contributes the most (9 of 11 severe rural crashes; PAF ≈ 36%).
Motorcycles are the most dangerous factor (OR ≈ 4.6); impairment and speeding ≈ 2.4×.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
Limitations

Few events: 36 severe crashes, 11 rural → wide intervals; only motorcycle clearly ≠ 1.
Duplicates affect Part I too: the MAR/MNAR files share the repeated crashes, so absolute scores are inflated (the comparison between treatments is still fair).
Association, not causation (darkness, zero-severe flags).
Missing variables: seat belts, curves, two-lane head-on risk, distance to trauma care.
Features selected on the full data → slightly optimistic scores.

title: Missing Data and Rural Crash Severity in Pennsylvania
text:
Take-aways

Complete-case removal is the most biased missing-data treatment, worst under MNAR. Prefer mean imputation over median for yes/no fields, and recover values from source fields when possible.
Accuracy misleads for a 5% outcome: always report precision, recall, F1 and AUC.
Ten mechanism-driven features beat the full set and a purely statistical pick (rural AUC 0.84).
On rural roads: aggressive driving contributes the most severe crashes; motorcycles are the most dangerous; impairment and speeding each ≈ 2.4×.
Next: multi-year data, seat-belt and road-geometry variables, and a rural-only model.
